lead: Two integrals, improper at the endpoints or at infinity for the parameter values that matter here, do a surprising amount of work. The gamma function turns the factorial into a smooth curve. The beta function measures how two powers of t and (1 − t) share the interval from 0 to 1. Together they evaluate a whole family of definite integrals that resist ordinary substitution, and they carry the constants of probability, statistics and physics. Some syllabi call them the Eulerian integrals. This chapter defines both, gives their main identities, and shows how to reduce a given integral to one of these two standard shapes.
prereq: You need: improper integrals and their convergence from Chapter 2.3, substitution from Chapter 2.2, and factorial notation.

blocks.text: Start with an integral over the whole positive axis.

blocks.where: t is the integration variable (t > 0); x is a real parameter; e<sup>−t</sup> is the decaying exponential; Γ is read "gamma of x".

blocks.text: The integral is improper at both ends. Near t = 0 the integrand behaves like tx−1, which is integrable exactly when x > 0. As t grows, e−t falls faster than any power of t, so the tail always converges. The limit comparison test of Chapter 2.3 gives this, and the domain is x > 0.

Two facts follow by direct work. Put x = 1: the integrand becomes e<sup>−t</sup>, and the integral is 1. Now take Γ(x+1) and integrate by parts with u = t<sup>x</sup> and dv = e<sup>−t</sup>dt. The bracket t<sup>x</sup>e<sup>−t</sup> vanishes at 0 and at ∞, and what remains is x times Γ(x).

blocks.where: the recurrence steps the argument up by 1 and multiplies by the old argument; Γ(1) = 1 is the starting value.

blocks.text: Apply the recurrence from Γ(1) again and again: Γ(n+1) = n! for every whole number n ≥ 0. So the gamma function is the factorial with the argument shifted by one. Γ(5) = 4! = 24, not 5!.
The half-integer value Γ(1/2) = √π is standard. It comes from the Gaussian integral and is needed whenever x is a half-integer.
The second function lives on the unit interval.

blocks.where: p > 0 and q > 0 are parameters; t is the integration variable; B is read "beta of p, q".

blocks.text: The interval is finite, but the integrand can blow up at an endpoint. Near t = 0 it behaves like t<sup>p−1</sup>, so we need p > 0. Near t = 1, write s = 1 − t; the integrand behaves like s<sup>q−1</sup>, so we need q > 0.
Put s = 1 − t, so dt = −ds. When t = 0, s = 1, and when t = 1, s = 0. The minus sign flips the limits 1 to 0 back to 0 to 1, and the two powers trade places. That proves the symmetry B(p,q) = B(q,p).
The beta function is not a new object at all. It is built from two gamma values.

blocks.where: the numerator holds the two separate gamma values and the denominator holds the gamma of the sum. The proof uses a double integral, so it is deferred; see Unit 5, Multiple Integrals.

sections.h3: Reducing an integral to beta or gamma form

items: Check the limits. 0 to 1 means beta; 0 to ∞ means gamma. Any other upper limit needs a substitution first.
For beta, force the integrand into the shape t<sup>p−1</sup>(1−t)<sup>q−1</sup> and read the two exponents. Add 1 to each exponent to get p and q.
For gamma, force the shape t<sup>x−1</sup>e<sup>−t</sup>. If the exponential is e<sup>−at</sup>, put u = at and divide the whole integral by a<sup>x</sup>.
Apply the formula, convert Γ(n+1) to n!, and simplify the fraction.

blocks.text: These two shapes cover a lot of ground. The normalising constant of the normal distribution, the density of the beta distribution in statistics, and many physics normalisations are beta or gamma integrals written in disguise.

figure.caption: B(2,3) runs through the gamma formula: Γ(2) = 1! and Γ(3) = 2! sit above Γ(5) = 4!, so the value is 2/24 = 1/12.

spec.aria: The block flow from Γ(5)=24 and B(2,3) to the beta formula, then to the substitution 1!·2!/4!, ending at 1/12.

examples.question: Using the gamma function, evaluate B(2,3) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> t(1−t)² dt, and confirm the value by expanding the integrand directly.
steps: Match the integrand with the beta definition: t<sup>p−1</sup> = t gives p = 2, and (1−t)<sup>q−1</sup> = (1−t)² gives q = 3. Both are positive, so the integral converges.
Convert each gamma value with Γ(n+1) = n!: Γ(2) = 1! = 1, Γ(3) = 2! = 2, Γ(5) = 4! = 24.
Direct check: (1−t)² = 1 − 2t + t², so the integrand is t − 2t² + t³. Its integral is t²/2 − 2t³/3 + t⁴/4 from 0 to 1, which is 1/2 − 2/3 + 1/4 = (6 − 8 + 3)/12 = 1/12.
examples.check:
import math

p, q = 2, 3
print(math.gamma(p) * math.gamma(q) / math.gamma(p + q))

examples.question: Evaluate ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> x²(1−x)³ dx using the beta function.
steps: The limits are 0 and 1 and the integrand already has the beta shape: x<sup>p−1</sup> = x² gives p = 3; (1−x)<sup>q−1</sup> = (1−x)³ gives q = 4.
So the integral equals B(3,4) = Γ(3)Γ(4)/Γ(7).
examples.check:
import math

p, q = 3, 4
print(math.gamma(p) * math.gamma(q) / math.gamma(p + q))

traps: Shift error on the factorial: Γ(n+1) = n!, so Γ(5) = 4! = 24 and Γ(2) = 1!, not 2!. Both the numerator and the denominator of the beta formula shift.
Reading p and q straight off the exponents: the exponent in the integrand is p − 1, so x² needs p = 3, not p = 2.
Missing the scale factor in the gamma form: ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> x<sup>n</sup>e<sup>−ax</sup>dx = Γ(n+1)/a<sup>n+1</sup>, so the power of a goes with the exponential, not just a plain division.
Using the beta formula when the limits are not 0 and 1, or the gamma formula when the upper limit is finite. Substitute first to reach the standard limits.
Treating Γ(0) as a number. Γ(x) → ∞ as x → 0<sup>+</sup>, so Γ(0) does not exist; the domain starts strictly above 0.

quiz.q: Define Γ(x) and B(p,q), stating the range of every parameter.
quiz.a: Γ(x) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> t<sup>x−1</sup>e<sup>−t</sup>dt for x > 0. B(p,q) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> t<sup>p−1</sup>(1−t)<sup>q−1</sup>dt for p > 0, q > 0.

quiz.q: Write down Γ(6), Γ(1/2) and B(1,1).
Which substitution proves B(p,q) = B(q,p)? Show the effect on the limits.
quiz.a: Put s = 1 − t, so dt = −ds. When t = 0, s = 1; when t = 1, s = 0. Flipping the limits removes the minus sign, and the integrand becomes s<sup>q−1</sup>(1−s)<sup>p−1</sup>, which is B(q,p).

quiz.q: Explain why the gamma integral converges exactly for x > 0.
quiz.a: Near t = 0 the integrand is close to t<sup>x−1</sup>, integrable only when x − 1 > −1, that is x > 0. At the upper end e<sup>−t</sup> decays faster than any power, so the tail converges for every x.
Put u = 2x, so dx = du/2 and x³ = u³/8. The integral becomes (1/16)∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup>u³e<sup>−u</sup>du = Γ(4)/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.

quiz.q: A student writes B(2,3) = Γ(2)Γ(3)/Γ(5) = 2!·3!/5!. Identify the three mistakes in the shift and give the correct value.
quiz.a: The shift is misapplied: Γ(2) = 1! = 1, not 2!, and Γ(3) = 2! = 2, not 3!. Also Γ(5) = 4! = 24, not 5!. The correct value is (1 × 2)/24 = 1/12.

quiz.q: By substituting t = u/(1+u), show that B(p,q) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> u<sup>p−1</sup>/(1+u)<sup>p+q</sup> du.
quiz.a: dt = du/(1+u)², and 1 − t = 1/(1+u). As t runs from 0 to 1, u runs from 0 to ∞. The integrand becomes u<sup>p−1</sup>/(1+u)<sup>p−1</sup> times 1/(1+u)<sup>q−1</sup> times 1/(1+u)², which collapses to u<sup>p−1</sup>/(1+u)<sup>p+q</sup>.

beyond: Not for the exam. The gamma function extends to complex arguments, where it has poles at 0, −1, −2, … and feeds the Riemann zeta function and the analytic theory of numbers. In statistics, the beta distribution on [0, 1] is used for proportions, and its density is exactly the beta integrand. Engineers meet gamma integrals in the normalisation of probability densities and in fractional calculus, where derivatives of non-integer order are defined through gamma ratios. Search next for "Euler gamma function complex plane", "beta distribution" and "Dirichlet integral".
